entries.lesson_core_move: Map each time feature in x(t) to t0/a in x(at) for a>1 and identify the resulting waveform as compressed toward t=0 with unchanged amplitudes.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Compression

blocks.text: When the signal is written as $y(t)=x(at)$ with $a>1$, read the factor $a$ as a horizontal compression. Every time feature at $t_0$ in $x(t)$ appears at $t_0/a$ in $y(t)$, and the amplitudes stay the same.
Start with the base case $y(t)=x(2t)$. Doubling the input time makes every feature happen at half its original time, so the waveform moves closer to $t=0$.
The same rule works for any $a>1$: solve $at=t_0$ for the new time, which gives $t=t_0/a$. That is the location of every feature in the compressed waveform.
So the result is a compressed version of $x(t)$ squeezed toward $t=0$, with the horizontal spacing reduced and the amplitudes unchanged.

sections.section_title: Recognizing x(at) as Time Compression for a>1

example_content.example_prompt: Given $y(t)=x(4t)$, determine whether the signal is compressed or expanded and state what happens to the feature at $t_0=6$.

explanation_blocks.text: Given $y(t)=x(4t)$, the factor $4>1$ means the signal is time-compressed toward $t=0$. The rule from the introduction applies: each time feature at $t_0$ moves to $t_0/4$ and keeps its amplitude.
For the marked feature at $t_0=6$, solve the matching time equation $4t=6$.
That gives $t=6/4=1.5$, so the feature appears earlier in time but has the same height.
So $x(4t)$ is a compressed version of $x(t)$, with every time coordinate divided by $4$ and every amplitude unchanged.

sections.section_title: Mapping a Single Time Feature Under Compression

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=6$, where does that peak appear in $x(3t)$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the factor inside the argument: $x(3t)$ means $a=3>1$, so the feature moves toward $t=0$ by dividing its time coordinate by $3$.
For the peak at $t_0=6$ in $x(t)$, match the same feature by setting the input-time equation $3t=6$.
Solving gives $t=2$, so the peak now appears at $t=2$ in $x(3t)$.
The peak height does not change; only its time location changes, so this is the same compression rule applied to one marked feature.

sections.section_title: Compressing Support Intervals and Durations

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[2,10]$, what is the support of $y(t)=x(2t)$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the support interval of $x(t)$ and the factor $2$ in $y(t)=x(2t)$. Because $a=2>1$, each support endpoint moves toward $t=0$ by dividing its time coordinate by $2$, and the amplitudes stay the same.
Start from the original support $[2,10]$. Map the left endpoint to $2/2=1$ and the right endpoint to $10/2=5$.
So the support of $y(t)$ is $[1,5]$. The duration changes from $10-2=8$ to $5-1=4$, which is half the original length, while the amplitudes stay unchanged.
This is the same compression rule applied to an entire interval: the support squeezes toward $t=0$, and only the horizontal spacing changes.

sections.section_title: Reading a Compressed Waveform with Unchanged Amplitudes

example_content.example_prompt: A waveform $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=4$ and is nonzero on $[1,7]$. Describe the waveform $y(t)=x(2t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the factor inside $y(t)=x(2t)$. Since $2>1$, read it as compression toward $t=0$: each time coordinate in $x(t)$ moves to half its original value, and the amplitudes stay the same.
Apply that rule to the peak at $t=4$: solve $2t=4$, so the peak moves to $t=2$. Apply the same rule to the support endpoints $1$ and $7$: they move to $1/2$ and $7/2$.
So the full compressed waveform has the same peak height as $x(t)$, but its nonzero interval is now $[1/2,7/2]$. Everything has moved inward by the same horizontal factor.
In one sentence, $y(t)=x(2t)$ is the original waveform squeezed toward $t=0$ with unchanged amplitudes, a peak at $t=2$, and support $[1/2,7/2]$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Map each time feature in x(t) to t0/a in x(at) for 0<a<1 and identify the resulting waveform as expanded away from t=0 with unchanged amplitudes.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Expansion

blocks.text: When you see $y(t)=x(at)$ with $0<a<1$, read it as time expansion. The waveform keeps the same amplitudes, but every time feature moves away from $t=0$.
Use $x(t/2)$ as the clean base case. Here $a=\tfrac{1}{2}$, so a feature that was at $t_0$ in $x(t)$ appears at $t_{new}=t_0/a=2t_0$ in $x(t/2)$.
The same $t_0/a$ rule applies to every other time feature, so the whole signal stretches horizontally. Only the time locations change; the heights stay the same.

sections.section_title: Recognizing x(t/2) as a Time Expansion

example_content.example_prompt: Decide whether $x(t/2)$ is a time expansion or a time compression, and state the stretch factor.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the fraction inside the argument. In $x(t/2)$, rewrite the signal as $x(at)$ with $a=\tfrac{1}{2}$. Because $0<a<1$, this is a time expansion.
Now check one landmark time. If a feature was at $t_0$ in $x(t)$, then in $x(at)$ it appears where $at=t_0$, so $t_{new}=t_0/a$.
So every time feature in the waveform moves twice as far from $t=0$ while its height stays the same. That is why $x(t/2)$ is a time expansion with stretch factor $2$.

sections.section_title: Mapping Original Time Points to t0/a

example_content.example_prompt: A feature is located at $t_0=-6$ in $x(t)$. If the signal becomes $x(t/3)$, where does that feature move, and what is the general rule for any $t_0$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the factor inside the argument. In $x(t/3)$, rewrite the signal as $x(at)$ with $a=\tfrac{1}{3}$, so the location rule is $t_0 \mapsto t_0/a$.
Now apply that rule to the labeled time point. Solving $at=t_0$ gives $(\tfrac{1}{3})t=-6$, so the same feature moves to $t_{new}=t_0/a=-18$.
The sign stays negative, but the point moves farther from $t=0$. That is the universal rule for this lesson: every original time point $t_0$ moves to $t_0/a$ when $0<a<1$.

sections.section_title: Finding Expanded Support with Unchanged Amplitude

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[1,3]$ and has peak amplitude $5$, find the support of $x(t/2)$ and state what happens to the amplitude.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the factor inside the argument. In $x(t/2)$, rewrite the signal as $x(at)$ with $a=\tfrac{1}{2}$. That means every original time point moves by the rule $t_{new}=t_0/a$.
Apply the rule to the support endpoints. The left endpoint $1$ moves to $1/(1/2)=2$, and the right endpoint $3$ moves to $3/(1/2)=6$, so the new support is $[2,6]$.
The interval widens away from $t=0$, but the waveform heights do not change. So the support expands to $[2,6]$ and the peak amplitude stays $5$.

entries.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
entries.lesson_core_move: Map each key time point t0 in x(t) to t0/a in x(at) by solving at=t0, then use that mapping to relocate starts, stops, corners, peaks, and zero crossings.

sections.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
sections.section_title: Introduction to How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points

blocks.text: When you see $x(at)$, the feature you are tracking stays the same feature, but its time coordinate changes. The cue is the scale factor inside the time argument, and the amplitude stays unchanged.
To find the new location, solve $at=t_0$ for $t$. That gives $t=t_0/a$, so the time point at $t_0$ in $x(t)$ appears at $t_0/a$ in $x(at)$.
Base case: a peak at $t_0=6$ in $x(t)$ moves to $t=3$ in $x(2t)$. The peak is still a peak, and its amplitude does not change; only the horizontal placement changes.

sections.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
sections.section_title: Mapping One Key Time Point in x(at)

example_content.example_prompt: In $x(t)$, a peak occurs at $t_0=6$. Where does that peak appear in $x(2t)$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the scale factor $2$ inside $x(2t)$. Use the same rule from the tutorial: keep the peak, solve $at=t_0$, and find the new time coordinate.
So the peak appears at $t=3$ in $x(2t)$. The peak itself does not change, and its amplitude stays the same; only the horizontal position moves.

sections.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
sections.section_title: Mapping Start and Stop Times

example_content.example_prompt: In $x(t)$, the signal is nonzero on $2 \le t \le 10$. Where is it nonzero in $x(2t)$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the nonzero support interval. Use the same rule from the tutorial: map each endpoint with $2t=t_0$ and then rewrite the new interval in order.
So the signal is nonzero on $1 \le t \le 5$ in $x(2t)$. The start and stop times move independently, and because the scale factor is positive, the interval keeps the same order.

sections.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
sections.section_title: Mapping Corners and Peaks

example_content.example_prompt: In $x(t)$, a piecewise waveform has a corner at $t=1$, a peak at $t=4$, and another corner at $t=7$. Where do these three features appear in $x(3t)$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a waveform with several labeled features. Use the same rule on each one: solve $3t=t_0$, keep the label, and map every original time to $t_0/3$.

So the corner at $t=1$ moves to $t=\frac{1}{3}$, the peak at $t=4$ moves to $t=\frac{4}{3}$, and the corner at $t=7$ moves to $t=\frac{7}{3}$. Listed left to right, the features stay in the same order because all three times are divided by the same positive factor.

sections.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
sections.section_title: Mapping Zero Crossings

example_content.example_prompt: In $x(t)$, the signal crosses zero at $t=-6$, $t=0$, and $t=9$. Where are the zero crossings in $x(3t)$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a set of zero-crossing times, including a negative time and the origin. Use the same rule on each one: solve $3t=t_0$ and map every crossing time to $t_0/3$.
So the zero crossings in $x(3t)$ are at $t=-2$, $t=0$, and $t=3$. The origin stays fixed, and the order is preserved because every time is divided by the same positive factor.

sections.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
sections.section_title: Rebuilding a Scaled Time Axis from Key Points

example_content.example_prompt: A signal in $x(t)$ has key points at $t=-4$ (zero crossing), $t=-1$ (corner), $t=2$ (peak), and $t=5$ (stop time). Rebuild the key-point axis for $x(2t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a mixed list of labeled key points. Use the same rule on each one: solve $2t=t_0$, keep the label attached, and then rebuild the axis from left to right.

So the scaled time axis for $x(2t)$ is zero crossing at $t=-2$, corner at $t=-\frac12$, peak at $t=1$, and stop time at $t=\frac52$. The labels stay attached, and the left-to-right order is preserved.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a piecewise signal x(t) into x(at) for a>0 by mapping each breakpoint t0 to t0/a and replacing t with at in the formula assigned to each scaled interval.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Scaling of Piecewise Signals

blocks.text: A piecewise signal under $x(at)$ keeps the same values on each piece, but it does not keep the same breakpoint locations. The thing to recognize first is the rule for where each piece starts and ends after scaling.

blocks.latex: x(t)=\begin{cases}f_1(t), & t_0\le t<t_1\\f_2(t), & t_1\le t<t_2\end{cases} \Rightarrow x(at)=\begin{cases}f_1(at), & t_0/a\le t<t_1/a\\f_2(at), & t_1/a\le t<t_2/a\end{cases}

blocks.text: To find a new breakpoint, solve $at=t_0$ for $t$. That gives $t=t_0/a$, so every original breakpoint moves to its divided-by-$a$ location while the formula on that interval is rewritten with $at$ inside it.

blocks.latex: x(t)=\begin{cases}2,& t<6\\-1,& t\ge 6\end{cases},\qquad x(3t)=\begin{cases}2,& t<2\\-1,& t\ge 2\end{cases}

blocks.text: That is the whole first rule: replace $t$ by $at$ inside each interval formula, and move each breakpoint from $t_0$ to $t_0/a$. When $a>1$, the pieces move closer to $t=0$ and the signal is compressed; when $0<a<1$, the pieces move farther apart and the signal is expanded.

sections.section_title: Scaling the Breakpoints of a Simple Piecewise Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Find the piecewise definition of $x(3t)$ for $x(t)=\begin{cases}2,& t<6\\-1,& t\ge 6\end{cases}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a two-piece constant signal with one breakpoint, and the scale factor inside the argument is $3$. To locate the new breakpoint in $x(3t)$, solve $3t=6$ so the old breakpoint at $6$ moves to $t=2$.
Because this is time scaling only, the values on the left and right pieces stay $2$ and $-1$. The breakpoint changes location, but the interval values do not.

sections.section_title: Rewriting Piecewise Formulas After Replacing t with at

example_content.example_prompt: Find $x(2t)$ for $x(t)=\begin{cases}t+1,& 0\le t<2\\3-t,& 2\le t<4\end{cases}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a two-piece signal whose formulas depend on $t$, so this example uses both parts of the rule at once: move the breakpoint and rewrite each formula with $2t$ inside it. To move the breakpoint, solve $2t=2$.

Now substitute $2t$ into each interval formula. The first piece $t+1$ becomes $2t+1$, and the second piece $3-t$ becomes $3-2t$. The interval order stays the same, but the breakpoint moves from $2$ to $1$.

sections.section_title: Time Compression of a Multi-Interval Piecewise Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Find $x(2t)$ for $$x(t)=\begin{cases}0,& t<1\\t-1,& 1\le t<3\\2,& t\ge 3\end{cases}$$.

explanation_blocks.text: The original breakpoints are $t=1$ and $t=3$. For $x(2t)$, the input to $x$ is $2t$, so each original breakpoint is reached when $2t$ equals that breakpoint.

Next rewrite the formula assigned to each interval. The first and last pieces stay $0$ and $2$ because they are constants. The middle formula $t-1$ becomes $2t-1$ after replacing the input variable with $2t$.
Finally express the interval conditions in terms of $t$. Dividing each breakpoint by $2$ compresses the signal toward the origin while preserving the left-to-right order of the pieces.

sections.section_title: Time Expansion of a Multi-Interval Piecewise Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Find $x(t/2)$ for $x(t)=\begin{cases}0,& t<1\\t-1,& 1\le t<3\\2,& t\ge 3\end{cases}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a three-piece signal, and the factor inside the argument is $1/2$. Because $1/2<1$, this is the expansion case: each breakpoint moves away from $t=0$ instead of toward it.
Now rewrite the formulas on each interval with $t/2$ inside them. The constant pieces stay $0$ and $2$, and the middle piece $t-1$ becomes $t/2-1$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert time-scaled exponentials by rewriting e^{s(at)} as e^{(as)t} and interpreting a as changing the growth, decay, or oscillation rate in continuous time.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Scaling of Exponentials

blocks.text: When the exponent contains a time-scaled input, rewrite the expression so the scale factor multiplies the exponent coefficient. The core identity is $e^{s(at)} = e^{(as)t}$, which keeps the exponential family the same while changing its rate.
Start with the real exponential $e^{-t}$. If you replace $t$ by $2t$, the result is $e^{-2t}$, so the same decay shape happens twice as fast and is compressed toward $t=0$.

That same rate change rule gives the general interpretation: if $a>1$, the exponential evolves faster, and if $0<a<1$, it evolves more slowly. The multiplier changes how quickly the curve moves in time, not the exponential family itself.

The same idea also applies when the exponent is imaginary. For a complex exponential, $e^{j\omega(at)} = e^{j(a\omega)t}$, so the factor $a$ changes the oscillation rate in exactly the same way that it changes the growth or decay rate in a real exponential.

sections.section_title: Rewriting a Time-Scaled Real Exponential

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $x(t)=e^{-3(2t)}$ in standard form and state how its decay compares with $e^{-3t}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the factor $2$ inside the exponent. For a time-scaled real exponential, rewrite the signal by multiplying the exponent coefficient by the scale factor.

Compared with $e^{-3t}$, the exponent coefficient changes from $-3$ to $-6$. The rewritten signal is still the same exponential family, but its decay happens twice as fast because the coefficient is larger in magnitude.
So the time-scaled signal is compressed toward $t=0$ and has unchanged amplitude. The only change is the decay rate, which is faster in the rewritten form $e^{-6t}$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Faster and Slower Exponential Decay

example_content.example_prompt: Compare $x_1(t)=e^{-2(3t)}$ and $x_2(t)=e^{-2(0.5t)}$ with the unscaled signal $e^{-2t}$; rewrite each and decide which decays fastest, which is unchanged, and which decays slowest.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the scale factor inside the exponent. Rewrite each signal by multiplying the base decay coefficient by that factor, then compare the resulting coefficients.
The effective decay coefficients are $-6$, $-2$, and $-1$. Since the more negative coefficient decays faster, $x_1(t)$ decays fastest, $e^{-2t}$ is unchanged, and $x_2(t)$ decays slowest.

That ordering matches the scaling rule: $a>1$ compresses the waveform toward $t=0$, while $0<a<1$ stretches it away from $t=0$. The same coefficient-multiplication rule explains both the rewrite and the decay-speed comparison.

sections.section_title: Scaling the Oscillation Rate of a Complex Exponential

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $x(t)=e^{j4(2t)}$ in standard form and state how the oscillation rate compares with $e^{j4t}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the factor $2$ inside the complex exponential. Use the same coefficient-multiplication rule as before: multiply the frequency coefficient by the time-scaling factor.

Compared with $e^{j4t}$, the angular frequency changes from $4$ to $8$. The rewritten signal is still the same complex exponential family, but it oscillates twice as fast because the coefficient was multiplied by $2$.

So the time-scaled complex exponential keeps the same amplitude while its oscillation rate increases. The general rule is still $e^{s(at)}=e^{(as)t}$; here the imaginary part of $s$ makes that rate change show up as faster oscillation.

sections.section_title: Scaling Both the Envelope and Oscillation of a Damped Sinusoid

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $x(t)=e^{(-1+j4)(2t)}$ in standard form and identify how both the envelope and oscillation compare with $e^{(-1+j4)t}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the scale factor $2$ multiplying $t$. Apply the same rule to every part of the complex exponent: multiply both the real part that controls decay and the imaginary part that controls oscillation.
The real part changes from $-1$ to $-2$, so the envelope is $e^{-2t}$ instead of $e^{-t}$ and decays twice as fast.
The imaginary part changes from $j4$ to $j8$, so the oscillation rate doubles. The initial amplitude is still $1$; time scaling changes the rate, not the starting height.
So the standard form is $e^{(-2+j8)t}$, and the combined interpretation is faster decay together with faster oscillation, exactly as the rule $e^{s(at)}=e^{(as)t}$ predicts.

entries.lesson_title: Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling
entries.lesson_core_move: Distinguish time shifts from time scaling by mapping transformed arguments to key-time locations and deciding whether features translate by a constant offset or compress/expand relative to t=0.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling
sections.section_title: Introduction to Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling

blocks.text: Track one labeled landmark in a reference signal. If $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=3$, that peak is the cue we will follow through both kinds of time transformation.

For a shift, the same landmark keeps its shape and moves by a constant offset. If the original peak is at $t=3$, then $x(t-t_s)$ places it at $t=3+t_s$, so every key time changes by the same additive amount.

For a scale with positive $a$, the landmark moves by multiplication instead of addition. If the original peak is at $t=3$, then $x(at)$ places it at $t=3/a$, so all landmark times are compressed or expanded relative to $t=0$.

Use this comparison test: the same additive offset means a time shift, while uniform multiplication or division of landmark times means time scaling. Shifts preserve spacing between features, but scaling changes spacing relative to $t=0$.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling
sections.section_title: Comparing One Key Time Under a Shift and a Scale

example_content.example_prompt: A signal $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=3$. Compare the peak location in $y_1(t)=x(t-2)$ and in $y_2(t)=x(4t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the peak at $t=3$ in the reference signal $x(t)$. For each transformed signal, match the inside argument to that original peak time and solve for $t$.
So the peak in $y_1(t)=x(t-2)$ lands at $t=5$. A shift adds the same constant offset to the landmark time.
So the peak in $y_2(t)=x(4t)$ lands at $t=\frac{3}{4}$. A scale divides the landmark time by the scale factor and pulls it toward $t=0$.
The contrast is the rule to remember: shifts add a constant offset to every key time, while scaling multiplies the argument and changes the key time by a factor.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling
sections.section_title: Comparing Multiple Key Times Under a Shift and a Scale

example_content.example_prompt: The signal $x(t)$ has key times at $t=2$, $t=4$, and $t=6$. Compare the key times in $y_1(t)=x(t-3)$ and in $y_2(t)=x(2t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the set of key times $t=2$, $t=4$, and $t=6$ in the reference signal $x(t)$. Use the same landmark rule as before: a shift adds the same offset to every key time, while a scale divides every key time by the scale factor.
So $y_1(t)=x(t-3)$ places the key times at $5$, $7$, and $9$. The gaps stay the same, so the whole pattern has shifted rigidly by a constant amount.
So $y_2(t)=x(2t)$ places the key times at $1$, $2$, and $3$. The gaps shrink from $2$ to $1$, so the pattern is compressed toward $t=0$.

The comparison rule is now visible in the spacing: equal additive offsets preserve the gaps, while uniform division changes the gaps. That is the cue for distinguishing a shift from a scale when more than one key time is present.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling
sections.section_title: Identifying Translation vs Compression from Key-Time Spacing

example_content.example_prompt: The signal $x(t)$ has key times at $t=1$ and $t=5$. One candidate transformed signal has them at $t=4$ and $t=8$; another has them at $t=1/2$ and $t=5/2$. Decide which candidate is a translation and which is a compression, and name the shift or scale factor.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the spacing between the key times. In the reference signal, the distance from $t=1$ to $t=5$ is $4$, so a translation must keep that gap unchanged, while a compression must change it by a uniform factor.
Candidate 1 keeps the spacing at $4$, so it is a translation. The key times move from $1$ and $5$ to $4$ and $8$, which is a shift right by $3$.
Candidate 2 cuts the spacing from $4$ to $2$, so it is a compression by factor $2$. The key times move from $1$ and $5$ to $1/2$ and $5/2$, which is the same as dividing every time by $2$.

So the classification is: candidate 1 is a translation with offset $3$, and candidate 2 is a compression with factor $2$. The spacing test is the rule to remember: unchanged gaps mean translation; uniformly reduced gaps mean compression.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling
sections.section_title: Distinguishing Shift and Scale in Piecewise Signals

example_content.example_prompt: The piecewise signal $x(t)$ equals $2$ from $t=1$ to $t=4$ and $0$ elsewhere. Compare the breakpoints in $y_1(t)=x(t-2)$ and $y_2(t)=x(2t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the breakpoint pair $t=1$ and $t=4$ that turns the level $2$ on and off. The original width is $4-1=3$, so a shift must move both breakpoints by the same offset, while a scale must solve the transformed argument at each breakpoint.
So $y_1(t)=x(t-2)$ is $2$ on the interval from $t=3$ to $t=6$ and $0$ elsewhere. The width stays $3$, so this is a translation by $2$.

So $y_2(t)=x(2t)$ is $2$ on the interval from $t=1/2$ to $t=2$ and $0$ elsewhere. The width shrinks from $3$ to $3/2$, so this is a compression by factor $2$. The piecewise levels stay the same; only the breakpoint locations change.

The comparison rule is now clear: equal additive offsets mean translation, while uniformly divided breakpoint spacing means compression or expansion. Use the breakpoints and the interval width to classify the transformed piecewise signal.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling
sections.section_title: Distinguishing Shift and Scale in Exponential Signals

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{-t}$, the value $e^{-2}$ occurs at $t=2$. Compare the time of that same level in $y_1(t)=x(t-2)$ and in $y_2(t)=x(3t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the level $e^{-2}$ in the exponential signal. For $x(t)=e^{-t}$, that level occurs at $t=2$, so we track the time at which the same level appears after each transformation.
So $y_1(t)=x(t-2)$ reaches the level $e^{-2}$ at $t=4$. The shift adds the same offset to the level time.
So $y_2(t)=x(3t)$ reaches the level $e^{-2}$ at $t=2/3$. The scale divides the original level time by $3$.

The comparison rule is the same one used before: a shift moves the landmark by addition, while a scale moves it by division. For an exponential signal, the landmark is a level rather than a geometric feature.
